statement: Two different squares of an 8 by 8 chessboard are chosen so that they share a side. How many such pairs of squares are there? (The order of the two squares does not matter.)

choices.misconception: I counted only pairs that sit side by side in a row, 7 in each of the 8 rows, and forgot pairs where one square is above the other.
I gave every square 4 neighbours and halved, but squares on the edge of the board have only 2 or 3 neighbours.
I added up the neighbours of every square but did not halve, so every pair was counted twice.
I gave all 64 squares 4 neighbours and did not halve.

hints: How many neighbours does a corner square have? An edge square? A middle square?
Count, for every square, how many squares share a side with it, and add these up. Then ask how many times each pair has been counted.
There are 4 corner squares with 2 neighbours, 24 other edge squares with 3, and 36 inner squares with 4. Each pair is counted once from each of its two squares.

solutions.reliable: Count neighbours square by square. The 4 corner squares have 2 neighbours each (8), the 24 other edge squares have 3 each (72), and the 36 inner squares have 4 each (144): 224 in total. Each pair has been counted twice, once from each of its squares, so there are 224 / 2 = 112 pairs. The transferable idea: when every object is counted the same number of times, count freely and then divide by that number.
solutions.elegant: Count by direction instead. Pairs side by side in a row: 7 in each of 8 rows, which is 56. Pairs one above the other: 7 in each of 8 columns, which is 56. Total 112, which checks the overcount.

whyOnTest: Overcount-then-correct questions test whether you can see how many times each object was counted, and the choices hold every way to get that factor wrong.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
